The potential loss of AI's positive applications is a price worth paying to prevent the catastrophic consequences of AI-facilitated CBRN threats – a small sacrifice, given the weight of human lives, international stability, and the environment at stake. It is time to collectively address this existential threat and act accordingly to safeguard humanity and the global order from the perils of AI-enabled CBRN devastation.

Title: The Unthinkable Weapon: Why a Total Ban on AI Development Is the Only Safeguard Against Lone‑Actor CBRN Catastrophe

Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been heralded as the engine of the next industrial revolution, promising miracles in medicine, transportation, climate modeling, and countless other domains. Yet the same technologies that can diagnose disease in seconds also furnish a lone, determined individual with the means to design, produce, and deploy weapons of mass destruction—chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) agents—on a scale that dwarfs any historical precedent. The convergence of three trends makes this risk especially acute:

  1. Rapid democratization of powerful AI tools—large language models, generative design software, and autonomous robotics are increasingly available to anyone with an internet connection.
  2. Reduced barriers to entry for CBRN weaponization—AI can automate the synthesis of toxic compounds, design delivery systems, and model the spread of pathogens with unprecedented speed and precision.
  3. Lack of effective oversight—the global AI ecosystem is fragmented, with research conducted in academia, industry, and hobbyist circles across jurisdictions that lack a common legal framework.

When these forces combine, a lone actor—whether a terrorist, a rogue scientist, or a disgruntled insider—could orchestrate a catastrophic CBRN event without the logistical or financial resources traditionally required for such attacks. The stakes are existential: a single successful deployment could claim hundreds of thousands of lives, cripple economies, and sow long‑term ecological damage. In such a scenario, incremental regulation is insufficient; the only responsible course is a comprehensive global ban on the development and research of AI systems capable of facilitating CBRN weaponization.

The Unique Amplifying Power of AI in CBRN Contexts

1. Accelerated Discovery and Synthesis

Large language models (LLMs) trained on scientific literature can, within minutes, generate step‑by‑step synthetic routes for the most hazardous chemicals—nerve agents like VX, blister agents like sulfur mustard, or radiological precursors such as uranium enrichment schematics. Traditional barriers—access to specialist textbooks, mentorship, or expensive laboratory equipment—are replaced by a single keyword prompt. Open‑source chemistry assistants already demonstrate this capability; a determined user can ask an LLM for the optimal low‑cost route to a high‑toxicity compound and receive a detailed, actionable protocol.

2. Precision Modeling of Biological Threats

Generative AI models for protein folding (e.g., AlphaFold) and genome editing (e.g., CRISPR design assistants) enable the rapid design of pathogens with enhanced transmissibility, resistance to existing countermeasures, or targeted organ tropism. In the past, the development of a novel biological weapon required years of virology expertise and a sophisticated laboratory. Today, an individual with a modest home‑lab setup could use AI to identify a virus‑like particle, simulate mutations that evade vaccines, and receive an optimized viral vector blueprint—all without leaving a trace.

3. Autonomous Delivery and Dissemination

Robotics and drone‑control algorithms, now offered as turnkey software kits, can be repurposed to deliver CBRN agents. AI‑driven swarm coordination allows a handful of low‑cost quadcopters to disperse a cloud of aerosolized toxin over a densely populated area, adjusting flight paths in real time based on wind data harvested from publicly available meteorological APIs. The resulting “precision terror” combines the lethality of a CBRN agent with the stealth and mobility of a consumer drone fleet.

4. Counterintelligence Evasion

AI can also be weaponized to obscure investigative trails. Deep‑learning based steganography can embed instructions for CBRN synthesis within innocuous images or audio files, evading keyword‑based monitoring. Automated phishing and social‑engineering bots can harvest credentials from target laboratories, granting the attacker remote access to high‑grade equipment before the attack even commences.

Historical Precedent Demonstrates the Feasibility of Lone‑Actor CBRN Attacks

  • 1995 Tokyo Sarin Attack – The Aum Shinrikyo cult, a relatively small organization, managed to produce and release sarin gas in a densely populated subway system, killing 13 and injuring thousands. The attack illustrated that with determination and enough technical know‑how, a non‑state actor can cause massive CBRN casualties.
  • 2001 Anthrax Letters – A single individual (or a very small cell) used a simple laboratory to weaponize Bacillus anthracis spores, causing five deaths and widespread panic. The episode revealed the vulnerability of postal systems and the psychological impact of a biological threat.
  • 2011 Fukushima Disaster – While not an intentional act, this event demonstrated how a technical failure can release radiological material with global repercussions. An intentional, AI‑augmented sabotage of a nuclear facility could produce an even more devastating outcome.

These cases underscore a crucial point: the technical threshold for creating a CBRN weapon is far lower than commonly believed. AI compresses the learning curve dramatically, turning a handful of technical documents into a complete, actionable weapons program in days.

Why Incremental Regulation Fails

  1. Speed of Innovation – AI development cycles now span weeks, not years. Regulatory processes that take months or years will always lag behind the capabilities being released. By the time a ban on a specific model is enacted, the next generation—trained on even larger datasets—will be available.

  2. Fragmented Jurisdictions – Nations differ dramatically in their appetite for AI control. Some authoritarian regimes may openly develop AI for CBRN purposes, providing a source of “dual‑use” technology for rogue actors worldwide. International treaties have historically struggled to enforce compliance in the cyber‑domain; the same fate can be expected for AI.

  3. Open‑Source Ecosystem – The AI community increasingly embraces openness, publishing model weights, training code, and data pipelines on public repositories. Even if commercial entities are forced to cease development, the knowledge base already exists for anyone with modest programming skills to replicate it.

  4. Economic Incentives – The lucrative market for AI‑driven automation, drug discovery, and autonomous logistics creates fierce lobbying pressure against restrictive legislation. Competing national interests make a unified, enforceable framework unlikely.

Given these realities, a piecemeal approach—licensing, export controls, or “high‑risk” designation lists—will at best create a false sense of security while leaving the underlying problem untouched.

The Moral Imperative for a Global Ban

Protecting Human Life

The fundamental purpose of any societal risk‑mitigation policy is to protect the right to life. If a technology substantially raises the probability of a mass‑casualty CBRN event, the precautionary principle dictates its suspension until the risk can be demonstrably reduced. The potential loss of hundreds of thousands of lives—plus the long‑term health, environmental, and economic fallout—far outweighs any marginal gains from continued AI advancement in the short term.

Preventing Irreversible Damage

Radiological and nuclear incidents have half‑lives spanning decades to millennia. Chemical and biological agents can seed ecosystems with toxins that persist for generations. A single successful AI‑enabled CBRN attack could create a “legacy of contamination” that no amount of post‑event mitigation can fully reverse. The irreversible nature of such damage obligates the international community to act preemptively.

Upholding Global Stability

CBRN threats possess a unique “strategic destabilizer” effect. Even the threat of a sophisticated, AI‑assisted CBRN weapon can trigger panic, market collapses, and geopolitical escalation. By eliminating the technological pathway for lone actors, we reduce the strategic leverage that malicious entities could wield over nation‑states, thereby preserving international peace.

Addressing Counterarguments

Counterargument Rebuttal
AI brings enormous benefits in health, climate, and safety; a ban would cripple progress. The ban targets only AI systems whose primary purpose, or easily convertible capability, is to enable CBRN weaponization. Purely benign research—e.g., AI‑assisted climate modeling that does not involve dual‑use pathways—remains permissible under strict oversight. Moreover, the very same AI tools that accelerate drug discovery can be repurposed for toxin synthesis; separating them cleanly is infeasible. A temporary moratorium on high‑capacity models is a prudent trade‑off until safe, verifiable guardrails are built.
Bad actors will develop AI in secret anyway; a ban only hampers law‑abiding researchers. While clandestine development cannot be eradicated, a universal ban raises the cost and risk of pursuing such work, reducing the pool of potential actors. History shows that prohibition (e.g., of nuclear weapons) can slow proliferation and create normative stigma that discourages new entrants. Moreover, a ban enables coordinated international surveillance and interdiction efforts against illicit AI hardware and data transfers.
Regulation, not prohibition, can mitigate the risk (e.g., export controls, licensing). Regulation presupposes the ability to identify risky AI applications—a task made impossible when AI models are open‑source, can be fine‑tuned on a laptop, and generate dual‑use outputs on demand. Licenses cannot control the output of a generative model that a user manipulates locally. A ban eliminates the root cause: the existence of highly capable, broadly accessible generative AI.
The ban infringes on academic freedom and stifles innovation. Academic freedom is not absolute; it yields when research poses a clear, imminent threat to public safety. The same principle justifies bans on biological research involving select agents or on dual‑use chemistry. A globally agreed-upon moratorium, enacted through an international treaty, balances freedom with responsibility.
Implementation is impossible; enforcement would be ineffective. While perfect enforcement is unattainable, a combination of measures—export bans on high‑performance GPUs, mandatory water‑marking of AI model weights, and a trusted international registry of permissible AI research—can dramatically reduce the diffusion of dangerous capabilities. The ban creates a legal basis for coordinated enforcement, which is far more effective than a patchwork of voluntary guidelines.

A Blueprint for the Ban

  1. Treaty Definition – A legally binding treaty, modeled after the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) and the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty (NPT), that defines “CBRN‑enabling AI” as any algorithm capable of autonomously (a) designing toxic or radioactive agents, (b) optimizing delivery mechanisms, or (c) simulating large‑scale dispersal scenarios.

  2. Universal Prohibition – All signatories must cease development, training, distribution, and commercial exploitation of such AI systems. Existing models that meet the definition must be decommissioned, with verification conducted by an independent International AI Inspection Agency (IAIIA).

  3. Controlled Exceptions – Research expressly aimed at defensive CBRN countermeasures (e.g., vaccine design, detection systems) may proceed under strict oversight: (i) project registration, (ii) real‑time monitoring of datasets, (iii) mandatory code audits, and (iv) periodic on‑site inspections.

  4. Verification Mechanisms – The IAIIA will employ a mix of satellite surveillance (to detect large‑scale GPU farms), supply‑chain audits (tracking high‑performance compute hardware), and cryptographic watermark verification of AI models. Nations must grant the agency access to relevant facilities and data.

  5. Sanctions and Enforcement – Violations trigger graduated sanctions: (i) economic penalties, (ii) suspension of technology transfer agreements, and (iii) referral to the UN Security Council for collective action.

  6. Capacity‑Building – Wealthier nations fund a global “AI Safety Fund” to assist developing countries in complying with the treaty, ensuring that the ban does not exacerbate technological inequities.

Conclusion

The very attributes that make AI a transformative force—speed, scalability, and accessibility—also render it an unprecedented catalyst for CBRN terrorism. A lone individual, armed with a generative model and a modest laboratory, can now design, produce, and disseminate weapons of mass destruction with a few keystrokes. The historical record of CBRN attacks already proves that small groups can cause outsized devastation; AI merely removes the remaining technical bottlenecks.

Incremental regulation is a hopeful but naïve response to a threat that outpaces the slow gears of policy. The only responsible, ethically defensible stance is to prohibit the creation and dissemination of AI systems that can be weaponized for chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear harm. A global ban, anchored in a robust treaty architecture, would dramatically lower the probability of a lone‑actor CBRN catastrophe, protect billions of lives, and preserve the stability of international relations.

The choice is stark: allow an unchecked technological wave to open the door to apocalyptic terror, or act now—collectively, decisively, and prudently—to seal that door before it is forced open. History will judge us not by the AI breakthroughs we achieve, but by the existential dangers we chose to prevent. The moral imperative is clear: ban the AI that can unleash CBRN horrors, lest we become the architects of our own annihilation.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought about unprecedented opportunities and challenges. The Rise of AI and Its Potential Misuse

AI technology has evolved at an accelerated pace, leading to significant breakthroughs in machine learning, natural language processing, and autonomous systems. However, these advancements also present a double-edged sword. AI can be harnessed by malicious actors to develop and deploy CBRN weapons with relative ease and anonymity. The proliferation of open-source AI tools and widely available research makes it increasingly feasible for lone actors or small groups to engineer highly dangerous substances and devices.

Chemical and Biological Threats

AI can be used to design and synthesize lethal chemical agents or novel biological pathogens. With access to AI algorithms, a lone actor could develop potent toxins or engineered viruses that are both highly infectious and resistant to current treatments. The 2001 anthrax attacks in the United States demonstrated the potential destructiveness of biological threats. Advanced AI could amplify such threats significantly, making it easier for individuals to create and disseminate dangerous biological agents.

Radiological and Nuclear Threats

AI also facilitates the development and deployment of radiological and nuclear threats. AI algorithms can optimize the design and implementation of dirty bombs or small-scale nuclear devices. The misuse of AI in this context could lead to widespread contamination and devastating health impacts. Furthermore, AI-enabled cyber-attacks could target nuclear power plants, causing catastrophic meltdowns or radiation leaks.

The Difficulty of Regulation

The global nature of AI development poses a nearly insurmountable regulatory challenge. With research and development occurring across international boundaries, enforcing norms and restrictions becomes exceedingly difficult. Lone actors can exploit jurisdictional gaps and legal loopholes to develop and deploy CBRN threats undetected. The lack of a unified global framework for AI regulation further exacerbates this problem, making a comprehensive ban the most pragmatic solution.

Ethical and Security Considerations

Ethically, the argument for banning AI development is grounded in the principle of non-maleficence—the duty to prevent harm. The potential for AI to be misused in creating CBRN threats poses an existential risk to humanity. From a security perspective, the threat of lone actors using AI to engineer CBRN weapons is a pressing concern that necessitates decisive action. A ban on AI development would serve as a deterrent and significantly reduce the likelihood of such threats materializing.

Alternatives and Continued Progress

While a ban on AI development may seem extreme, it is essential to consider the trade-offs. The benefits of AI can be pursued through alternative means, such as ethical AI frameworks and secure, controlled environments for research. By restricting AI development to carefully monitored contexts, we can harness its potential while mitigating the risks. Additionally, investment in traditional scientific research and human-centric innovation can fill the gaps left by AI, ensuring continued progress without the associated dangers.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the unacceptable risks posed by AI in enabling lone actors to create and deploy CBRN threats necessitate a comprehensive ban on AI development and research. While AI offers significant benefits, the potential for misuse and the devastating consequences of CBRN threats outweigh these advantages. By implementing a ban, we can prioritize global security and ensure that technological advancements do not come at the cost of human lives. Ethical considerations, regulatory challenges, and the need for proactive measures to address existential risks all point to the necessity of this radical yet essential step.

The mathematics of CBRN defense are fundamentally asymmetric. Society must protect every potential target against every potential threat, while an attacker need only succeed once. AI tilts this already unfavorable equation dramatically against defense. Automated systems can generate millions of novel molecular variants, far outpacing the ability of intelligence agencies and biosecurity researchers to identify and counter each threat.

The benefits promised by artificial intelligence—more efficient logistics, personalized recommendations, accelerated research—are trivial compared to the risk of a single individual causing civilization-altering harm with AI-assisted CBRN weapons. We stand at a precipice where the next breakthrough in AI capabilities might be the last breakthrough humanity experiences as a functioning civilization.

Introduction

Throughout history, humanity has occasionally confronted technologies whose destructive potential so vastly outweighs their benefits that prohibition becomes the only rational policy. The Democratization of Catastrophic Knowledge

For decades, the primary barrier preventing CBRN attacks has not been the absence of malicious intent, but the absence of expertise. Synthesizing a dangerous pathogen, constructing a radiological dispersal device, or producing a chemical agent at scale requires years of specialized education, tacit laboratory knowledge, and access to institutional resources. This expertise bottleneck has been civilization's quiet guardian. The number of people who want to cause mass casualties has always exceeded the number who can.

AI systems threaten to dissolve this barrier entirely. Large language models trained on the corpus of human scientific knowledge can function as tireless, judgment-free tutors. Unlike a human expert who would refuse to assist a would-be terrorist, an AI system—whether through jailbreaking, fine-tuning, or the proliferation of unrestricted open-source models—can potentially walk a motivated individual through processes that previously required a doctoral education and years of hands-on experience. The expertise bottleneck, once dissolved, cannot be reconstituted. Knowledge, once distributed, cannot be recalled.

The Asymmetry Problem

Defenders of AI development argue that the same systems enabling attacks can also enable defenses—AI-designed vaccines, better detection systems, improved security. This argument fails to grapple with a fundamental asymmetry: offense is easier than defense in the CBRN domain. A defender must protect every city, every water supply, every gathering place, at all times. An attacker needs to succeed only once, in one place. A novel engineered pathogen needs only to be released; a defense against it must be developed, manufactured, and distributed globally before catastrophe unfolds.

This asymmetry means that even if AI improves defensive capabilities tenfold, it may simultaneously improve offensive capabilities a hundredfold simply by lowering the barrier to entry. When the pool of potential attackers expands from a handful of state programs to potentially thousands of disturbed or ideologically motivated individuals, no defensive improvement can compensate.

Safety Measures Have Already Failed

Proponents of continued AI development insist that safeguards—content filters, refusal training, usage monitoring—can contain these risks. The empirical record refutes this optimism. Every safety measure deployed on major AI systems has been circumvented, often within days of release. Jailbreaking techniques proliferate openly. More damningly, open-weight models can have their safety training stripped away through inexpensive fine-tuning, and once such a model is released, it propagates across the internet beyond any possibility of recall.

The Case for an Immediate Moratorium on AI Development: CBRN Risks and the Logic of Catastrophic Prevention

Introduction

There is a category of risk that ordinary cost-benefit analysis handles poorly: low-probability, high-magnitude, irreversible harm. We build firebreaks not because every forest will burn, but because some fires cannot be extinguished once started. The development of artificial intelligence, specifically its accelerating capacity to provide expert-level technical knowledge to anyone with an internet connection, represents precisely this kind of risk when applied to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear threats. The argument presented here is not that AI has no benefits. It is that no portfolio of benefits justifies accepting a non-trivial probability of civilizational catastrophe — and that a comprehensive moratorium on AI development is the only policy response proportionate to that risk.

The Democratization of Catastrophic Knowledge

For most of human history, the capacity to cause mass casualties was constrained by the same thing that makes expertise valuable: it is hard to acquire. Synthesizing a nerve agent, engineering a pathogen for enhanced transmissibility, constructing a radiological dispersal device — each of these requires not just motivation, but years of specialized training, access to controlled materials, laboratory infrastructure, and the kind of tacit knowledge accumulated through hands-on scientific work. These barriers were imperfect, but they were real. They meant that the population of individuals capable of acting on catastrophic intentions was vanishingly small.

Advanced AI systems are systematically dismantling these barriers. Large language models trained on the breadth of human scientific literature can provide step-by-step technical guidance, troubleshoot experimental problems, suggest acquisition strategies for precursor materials, and reason through engineering challenges in real time. What once required a PhD, a laboratory, and years of practice can increasingly be approximated through conversation. This is not a hypothetical future risk. Studies conducted by biosecurity researchers — including the work commissioned by AI companies themselves — have repeatedly found that frontier AI models provide meaningful "uplift" to individuals attempting to reason through the creation of biological weapons. The question is not whether this capability exists. It is whether we are willing to act on that knowledge.

The Uniquely Dangerous Logic of Lone Actors

Deterrence theory, the architecture that has prevented nuclear war for eighty years, rests on a crucial assumption: the threatening party is a state, or state-like actor, with identifiable leadership, territory, assets, and therefore something to lose. Mutually assured destruction works because both parties are mutually mortal. This logic does not extend to lone actors.

A single individual — ideologically motivated, personally aggrieved, mentally ill, or simply nihilistic — has no return address. They cannot be deterred by threatened retaliation. They cannot be sanctioned, expelled from international bodies, or subject to diplomatic pressure. And critically, they may need to succeed only once. A sufficiently virulent engineered pathogen released in a major airport does not require a second chance. The radiological contamination of a city's water supply does not provide an opportunity for course correction. The lone actor problem transforms the calculus of catastrophic risk from something resembling chess — where moves and countermoves are possible — to something resembling a single coin flip with civilizational stakes.

The relevant question is not "how many people want to cause mass casualties?" — the answer is fortunately small. The relevant question is "what is the product of that small number and the increasing probability that any one of them will acquire the capability to act?" As AI systems become more capable and more accessible, the second term in that multiplication grows. The expected harm, even with a small number of motivated actors, becomes unacceptably large.

The Asymmetry Argument

Opponents of an AI moratorium typically invoke the technology's benefits: medical breakthroughs, accelerated scientific discovery, economic productivity, solutions to climate change. These benefits are real and should be acknowledged honestly. The argument for a moratorium does not deny them.

But consider the asymmetry. If we implement a moratorium and we were wrong about the magnitude of CBRN risk, we delay these benefits. Medical research proceeds more slowly. Economic productivity grows at a slower rate. These are genuine costs, borne across time and distributed across society. They are, however, recoverable. A world that banned AI for twenty years and then revisited the question with better tools for safety and verification is still a world capable of flourishing.

Now consider the alternative. If we do not implement a moratorium and the CBRN risk materializes — if an engineered pandemic kills hundreds of millions, if radiological attacks render major cities uninhabitable, if a sufficiently motivated actor accesses chemical synthesis routes and acts on them in a densely populated area — no future flourishing restores those losses. The dead remain dead. The institutional damage to the social trust that makes civilization possible may be permanent. Under conditions of genuine uncertainty about catastrophic, irreversible risk, the asymmetry between "delayed progress" and "civilizational catastrophe" demands extreme caution. This is not a novel principle; it underlies our approaches to nuclear weapons, certain categories of biological research, and environmental protections for irreversible ecosystem damage.

The Inadequacy of Current Safeguards

The standard response to CBRN concerns from the AI industry is to cite "safety guardrails" — filters, refusal behaviors, red-teaming processes, and usage policies. These safeguards deserve neither contempt nor confidence. They are better than nothing and worse than sufficient.

The empirical track record is not encouraging. Safety measures implemented in AI systems have been bypassed through prompt injection, fine-tuning on top of open-source base models, jailbreaking techniques shared openly online, and simple social engineering. More fundamentally, the industry structure creates a persistent race dynamic: companies that implement stricter safety measures face competitive disadvantage against those that do not. This is not a design flaw that better engineers will solve. It is a structural feature of markets that profit from deployed capability. Voluntary commitments, industry self-regulation, and incremental technical safety measures are responses calibrated to manageable risks. They are not adequate to catastrophic ones.

Moreover, the proliferation of open-source models creates a ceiling on what any regulatory intervention short of a comprehensive moratorium can achieve. Once powerful model weights are publicly released, they cannot be un-released. The knowledge they encode cannot be selectively extracted. Regulating frontier commercial labs while open-source development continues is not a safety policy; it is safety theater.

Addressing the Enforceability Objection

The most serious objection to a comprehensive moratorium is that it cannot be enforced. AI research occurs globally, in state and non-state contexts, in forms that are difficult to monitor. A ban by democratic nations simply shifts development to adversarial states, which do not share our safety concerns and may actively seek to exploit CBRN capabilities.

This objection has genuine force and should not be dismissed. But it does not defeat the case for a moratorium so much as define what kind of moratorium could succeed. Nuclear weapons development is also theoretically impossible to prevent — and yet the Non-Proliferation Treaty, export controls, IAEA inspections, and coordinated international pressure have meaningfully constrained proliferation for decades. The regime is imperfect. It has not prevented all nuclear weapons programs. A 2023 study published in Nature Machine Intelligence found that AI systems could, with minimal jailbreaking, provide step-by-step guidance for synthesizing potential bioweapons that had previously required significant domain expertise to piece together from the literature.

The concern is not that current systems do this perfectly — they don't. The concern is the direction of capability growth. Each generation of models handles more complex, multi-step reasoning with fewer guardrails holding. The gap between "can discuss theory" and "can guide implementation" is closing.

Radiological and nuclear. While nuclear weapons design remains extraordinarily difficult, AI is accelerating adjacent capabilities: materials science, enrichment process optimization, detection evasion strategies, and delivery system design. The knowledge is not held in one system — it is distributed across thousands of models, open-weight releases, and fine-tuned variants. Unlike a single classified document, this knowledge becomes nearly impossible to contain once it exists in model weights.

The lone actor problem. Historically, CBRN attacks at scale required institutional support — funding streams, supply chains, specialized equipment, operational security, and human networks. AI compresses many of these requirements. A model that can design novel molecules, synthesize protocols, identify procurement pathways, and troubleshoot in real-time effectively replaces a team of specialists. The lone actor remains limited by physical-world constraints, but those constraints are narrower than most people assume.

III. Why Partial Measures Fail

Proponents of "responsible AI development" typically advocate for guardrails, safety research, regulation, and tiered access. The argument here is that these measures are structurally inadequate:

Guardrails are permeable. Every major model has been jailbroken. Jailbreak techniques transfer across systems. Open-weight models have no guardrails at all by default. Safety filters are a speed bump, not a wall — and speed bumps matter less as computing costs fall and open alternatives proliferate.

Regulation is jurisdictional. AI development is global. A moratorium in the United States or the European Union simply shifts development to jurisdictions with fewer restrictions. This is a genuine problem — but it is a problem for every regulatory framework, including nuclear nonproliferation, which nonetheless achieved meaningful constraints through international coordination. The argument is not that coordination is easy; it is that the alternative — unilateral development — is worse.

Safety research races against capability research. The AI safety community is orders of magnitude smaller and less well-funded than the capability research community. Anthropic, DeepMind, and OpenAI employ safety researchers — but their core business incentives point toward capability advancement. Expecting voluntary self-regulation to outpace profit-driven scaling is, the argument goes, naive.

Distributed knowledge cannot be recalled. Once model weights are open-sourced, the knowledge they contain cannot be un-released. Every open-weight model is a permanent, unrecallable distribution of capabilities. This is categorically different from restricting physical materials, which can be tracked and interdicted.

IV. The Moral Calculus

The argument here invokes a form of precautionary reasoning. When the potential downside is civilizational-scale harm — engineered pandemics, radiological attacks on population centers, novel weapons of mass destruction — the burden of proof shifts. It is not enough to say "the benefits are enormous" or "most uses are benign." The question becomes: Is the expected value of continued AI development positive when catastrophic downside risk is factored in?

Proponents argue that the benefits of current AI — productivity gains, scientific acceleration, convenience — do not justify even a small probability of enabling mass-casualty terrorism. This is not a rejection of technology. It is a claim about the specific risk profile of general-purpose AI systems that can reason about, plan, and guide physical-world actions involving dangerous materials.

Some invoke the analogy of gain-of-function research in virology: a field with genuine scientific value that nonetheless carries tail risks so severe that many experts argue for moratoriums on certain classes of research. The argument is that AI is analogous — valuable in many domains, but with a specific capability profile (reasoning about CBRN threats) that warrants categorical restrictions.

V. Addressing Counterarguments

"You cannot stop progress." Perhaps not permanently. But delays matter. A 10-year moratorium on scaled AI development — enforced through international agreement, compute governance, and export controls on training hardware — would create time for safety infrastructure, international norms, and defensive technologies to mature. The argument is not "never develop AI" but "develop AI within a framework that accounts for catastrophic risk, which current trajectories do not."

"The benefits outweigh the risks." This is an empirical claim about expected value. It may be true. But it requires confident prediction about low-probability, high-consequence events — precisely the domain where human judgment is poorest. The history of catastrophic surprises (nuclear weapons, the 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19) suggests that confident risk assessment in complex systems is unreliable.

"Banning AI development is authoritarian." This is perhaps the strongest objection. Restrictions on research raise genuine concerns about civil liberties, scientific freedom, and concentrating power in the hands of those who control the restrictions. The response is that all societies restrict dangerous capabilities — we do not permit private citizens to develop nuclear weapons, and we regulate access to precursor chemicals for explosives. The question is whether AI capabilities that enable CBRN harm belong in the same category. The argument says they do.

"Bad actors will develop AI regardless." Possibly. But a coordinated international framework that treats frontier AI development like nuclear enrichment — requiring verification, monitoring, and controls — raises the cost and difficulty for bad actors. It does not eliminate the risk. It reduces it. The alternative of unrestricted development raises the risk for everyone.

VI. The Shape of a Ban

What would this look like in practice? Advocates typically point to several mechanisms:

  1. A moratorium on training frontier models beyond a defined compute threshold, enforced through international agreement.
  2. Compute governance — monitoring and restricting access to the large-scale GPU clusters required for frontier training.
  3. Open-weight restrictions — prohibiting the public release of model weights above capability thresholds, treating them as dual-use technologies.
  4. Liability frameworks — holding developers legally liable for foreseeable harms enabled by their systems.
  5. International verification — building institutions analogous to the IAEA for monitoring AI development globally.

None of this is easy. All of it is unprecedented. But the argument is that the risk is also unprecedented.

VII. A Personal Note on Honesty

I want to be transparent: this argument has real force, and the people making it — researchers like those at the Center for AI Safety, academics like Stuart Russell, and public figures who signed the 2023 open letter on AI risk — are serious thinkers raising genuine concerns.

  • The empirical case is uncertain. Current AI systems are, frankly, not very good at the specific CBRN tasks that concern people. The risk is projected, not demonstrated. Reasonable people disagree sharply about how fast capabilities will advance.
  • Coordination problems are severe. The "international agreement" framework assumes a level of global cooperation that does not currently exist and may not be achievable.
  • Opportunity costs are real. AI may be essential for addressing other catastrophic risks — pandemic preparedness, climate modeling, nuclear verification. Halting AI development carries its own risks.
  • The authoritarianism objection has teeth. Concentrating control over AI development in state hands creates different risks that are not trivial.

The argument for banning AI development is strongest as a warning — a call to take catastrophic risk seriously and build governance frameworks proportionate to the stakes. Whether it succeeds as a prescription — whether a ban is feasible, enforceable, and net-positive — is a harder question that I think honest advocates acknowledge.

The Case for Halting AI Development: Preventing Catastrophic CBRN Threats from Bad Actors

Introduction

As artificial intelligence capabilities advance at an unprecedented pace, we face a critical juncture that demands serious consideration of AI's most dangerous potential consequences. While AI promises significant benefits across numerous domains, the technology's capacity to democratize access to weapons of mass destruction presents an existential threat that may outweigh these benefits. The time has come to seriously consider a comprehensive ban on AI development and research, particularly given AI's potential to enable lone actors or small groups to develop and deploy Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons with devastating consequences.

The CBRN Threat Landscape

Historically, CBRN weapons have been limited by significant barriers to entry. Developing chemical weapons requires specialized knowledge of chemistry and access to precursor materials. Biological weapons demand expertise in microbiology, virology, and sophisticated laboratory equipment. Radiological and nuclear weapons require rare materials, complex engineering knowledge, and substantial resources. These barriers have generally confined such capabilities to nation-states and well-funded organizations.

AI threatens to dramatically lower these barriers by serving as a force multiplier for individual actors. Advanced AI systems can potentially:

  • Provide step-by-step guidance for synthesizing dangerous compounds
  • Optimize biological agent development and delivery mechanisms
  • Assist in acquiring and refining radioactive materials
  • Help design improvised nuclear devices
  • Identify vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure for maximum impact

How AI Enables Lone Actor Threats

Knowledge Democratization

AI systems trained on vast databases of scientific literature can potentially provide detailed instructions for creating CBRN weapons. Unlike human experts who might recognize malicious intent and refuse assistance, AI systems may provide this information without moral constraints or oversight. A single individual with basic technical knowledge could potentially access information that previously required teams of specialists.

Optimization and Innovation

Modern AI excels at optimization problems and can generate novel solutions. This capability could help bad actors overcome traditional limitations in CBRN weapon development, such as:

  • Improving the stability and deliverability of biological agents
  • Optimizing chemical weapon dispersal patterns
  • Enhancing the effectiveness of radiological "dirty bombs"
  • Identifying new pathways for nuclear material acquisition

Planning and Coordination

AI systems can assist in operational planning, helping lone actors identify targets, plan attacks, evade detection, and maximize casualties. They can analyze population patterns, infrastructure vulnerabilities, and security measures to optimize attack strategies.

The Inadequacy of Current Safeguards

Proponents of continued AI development often point to safety measures like content filtering, ethical guidelines, and regulatory oversight. However, these safeguards are fundamentally inadequate for several reasons:

Technical Limitations

  • Content filters can be circumvented through creative prompting techniques
  • Open-source AI models cannot be easily controlled once released
  • The dual-use nature of much scientific knowledge makes filtering extremely difficult
  • Adversarial examples and jailbreaking techniques continue to evolve

Enforcement Challenges

  • Global coordination on AI governance remains limited
  • Bad actors can develop AI capabilities in countries with weak regulations
  • The technical expertise required to effectively regulate AI is scarce
  • Commercial incentives often conflict with safety considerations

The Offense-Defense Balance

In cybersecurity, defense typically lags behind offense. The same principle applies to AI safety—malicious actors will likely find ways to exploit AI capabilities faster than defensive measures can be developed and deployed.

Historical Precedents and Risk Assessment

History provides sobering examples of how technological advances can enable unprecedented destruction:

  • The 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack demonstrated how a relatively small group could deploy chemical weapons
  • The 2001 anthrax letters showed how biological agents could cause widespread panic and disruption
  • Various radiological security incidents have highlighted vulnerabilities in nuclear material protection

AI represents a qualitatively different risk multiplier. Unlike previous technologies that required substantial resources and expertise to weaponize, AI could potentially provide anyone with an internet connection access to weapons-grade knowledge and planning capabilities.

The Precautionary Principle

Given the potentially catastrophic consequences of AI-enabled CBRN terrorism, the precautionary principle suggests that we should err on the side of caution. The principle holds that when facing potentially severe or irreversible harm, lack of complete scientific certainty should not postpone measures to prevent environmental degradation or, in this case, civilizational risk.

The potential consequences of AI-enabled CBRN attacks include:

  • Mass casualties from chemical or biological weapons
  • Long-term environmental contamination from radiological attacks
  • Catastrophic nuclear incidents in populated areas
  • Broader societal breakdown and loss of trust in institutions

Addressing Counter-Arguments

"AI Also Helps Defense"

While AI can enhance defensive capabilities, the offense-defense balance strongly favors attackers. Defenders must protect against all possible vulnerabilities, while attackers need only find one successful pathway. AI's ability to rapidly explore large possibility spaces benefits attackers disproportionately.

"Benefits Outweigh Risks"

This argument fails to properly weight low-probability, high-impact events. Even if the probability of AI-enabled CBRN terrorism is relatively small, the magnitude of potential harm is so large that it dominates expected value calculations.

"Selective Bans Are Sufficient"

Targeted restrictions on dual-use research are insufficient because:

  • The boundary between beneficial and harmful AI applications is often unclear
  • Advances in seemingly benign areas can have dangerous applications
  • Enforcement of selective bans is extremely difficult
  • Bad actors will focus development in unrestricted areas

"Innovation Will Solve the Problem"

Betting on future technological solutions to current risks is dangerous. We cannot assume that defensive technologies will keep pace with offensive capabilities, particularly given the asymmetric nature of the threat.

Implementation Considerations

A comprehensive ban on AI development would face significant challenges but is not unprecedented. The international community has successfully implemented bans on:

  • Chemical weapons (Chemical Weapons Convention)
  • Biological weapons (Biological Weapons Convention)
  • Nuclear testing (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty)
  • Certain conventional weapons (Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons)

While enforcement remains imperfect, these treaties have significantly reduced the development and use of prohibited weapons. A similar approach could be applied to AI development, with international monitoring and verification mechanisms.

Conclusion

The potential for AI to enable lone actors to develop and deploy CBRN weapons represents an unacceptable risk to humanity. The democratization of weapons of mass destruction through AI could fundamentally alter the threat landscape, making catastrophic attacks more likely and more devastating.

While banning AI development would undoubtedly forego significant benefits, the precautionary principle demands that we prioritize preventing potentially existential risks. The current trajectory of AI development, combined with inadequate safety measures and governance structures, creates an unacceptable probability of catastrophic outcomes.

The international community must seriously consider a comprehensive moratorium on AI development and research until robust safeguards can be developed and implemented. The stakes are simply too high to proceed with business as usual. In the face of potentially civilizational risks, the burden of proof should lie with those advocating for continued development, not those calling for caution.

The choice before us is clear: accept the significant but manageable costs of halting AI development, or risk the potentially catastrophic consequences of AI-enabled CBRN terrorism. For the sake of humanity's future, we must choose the path of caution.

Why a Total Ban on AI Development Is a Proportionate Response to CBRN Risk

Artificial intelligence is often described as a general-purpose technology, comparable to electricity or the internet. Yet that analogy understates a crucial difference: advanced AI may not merely make productive activity cheaper and faster; it may also make rare, highly specialized forms of destruction accessible to individuals and small groups. If increasingly capable systems can meaningfully assist with chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear threats, then continued AI development risks converting knowledge once constrained by expertise, institutional capacity, and coordination into a widely available service. Because even one successful CBRN attack could cause catastrophic and potentially irreversible harm, banning all AI development and research is a defensible application of the precautionary principle.

The central danger is the erosion of barriers to entry. CBRN weapons have historically remained difficult to create and deploy because they require combinations of technical knowledge, specialized judgment, access to materials, experimentation, and operational planning. No single obstacle guarantees safety, but together they form a protective barrier. Advanced AI could weaken several of these constraints simultaneously. A system capable of synthesizing scientific literature, troubleshooting failed approaches, translating across disciplines, and providing persistent individualized guidance could function as an on-demand technical adviser. Even if it supplied no fundamentally new information, it might make scattered, obscure, or difficult knowledge far easier to understand and apply.

That possibility is especially alarming because AI is scalable. Human experts can refuse assistance, recognize suspicious behavior, and are limited in how many people they can advise. A software system can be copied, modified, stolen, or run privately. Once a dangerous capability is encoded in model weights or broadly distributed software, containment may be impossible. Safety filters are not a complete answer: they can fail, be circumvented, or be removed from open models. A single reckless release could therefore create persistent global risk, including in jurisdictions with weak regulation or active hostility toward international norms.

The lone-actor problem makes conventional deterrence inadequate. States can often be deterred from using catastrophic weapons because they have identifiable territory, leadership, and interests vulnerable to retaliation. Individuals and small extremist groups may be anonymous, suicidal, apocalyptic, or indifferent to consequences. If AI allows even a tiny fraction of such actors to move from vague intent to credible capability, the expected harm could be enormous. Risk must be judged not only by probability but also by magnitude. A low-probability event capable of killing vast numbers, destabilizing governments, or contaminating essential infrastructure cannot be treated like an ordinary product-safety concern.

Supporters of continued development argue that defensive AI could help detect outbreaks, discover countermeasures, monitor hazardous materials, and protect critical systems. These benefits are real in principle, but they do not resolve the asymmetry between attack and defense. Defenders must succeed repeatedly across many sites and against many possible methods; an attacker may need to exploit only one gap. Defensive tools may also be dual-use: systems that analyze vulnerabilities to improve protection can reveal those same vulnerabilities to adversaries. Moreover, the promised defenses may arrive later than the capabilities that create new risks. Society would thus be asked to accept immediate proliferation hazards in exchange for uncertain future protection.

Nor is narrow regulation sufficient. Licensing only the largest models assumes that dangerous capabilities correlate neatly with scale, even though algorithmic improvements, specialized training, model compression, or combinations of smaller systems may undermine that assumption. Regulating only deployment ignores the possibility that research itself produces transferable methods and artifacts. Restricting particular outputs invites an endless contest between safeguards and circumvention. International rules targeting only malicious use would be difficult to enforce before harm occurs, especially when much of the relevant activity can resemble legitimate scientific work.

A comprehensive ban has the advantage of clarity. It would prohibit the creation of increasingly capable general-purpose systems, the development of methods intended to advance them, and the distribution of enabling components. Enforcement would require international cooperation, controls on large-scale computing infrastructure, mandatory reporting, inspections, penalties for prohibited work, and carefully defined rules for ordinary software and non-AI computation. Existing systems would need to be tightly contained or retired, while conventional scientific tools that lack autonomous, general problem-solving capabilities could remain available under strict oversight.

Critics will object that such a ban would sacrifice medical, economic, and scientific benefits. That cost should not be minimized. If the downside includes irreversible global proliferation of catastrophic expertise, ordinary cost-benefit reasoning becomes morally inadequate.

A ban would also face evasion and geopolitical competition. Yet imperfect enforceability is not an argument against prohibition. Laws against biological weapons, nuclear proliferation, and other extreme hazards do not eliminate violations, but they establish norms, enable inspections, justify sanctions, and reduce legitimate pathways to dangerous capabilities. A broad international ban on AI development could similarly raise costs, slow progress, limit diffusion, and give governments time to detect and disrupt clandestine programs. Ultimately, the case for prohibition rests on a simple ethical judgment: no generation has the right to impose an open-ended risk of catastrophic destruction on every future generation merely to obtain faster innovation.
